titre: Marie Tharp, the Valley Her Colleague Refused to Believe
accroche: In 1952, a cartographer spots a rift in the middle of the Atlantic. Her colleague takes a year to believe her; he had dismissed it as “girl talk.”
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1952, at the Lamont Geological Observatory at Columbia University, a young cartographer named Marie Tharp draws, bathymetric profile after bathymetric profile, the relief of the Atlantic Ocean floor. The data come from the precision depth sounders aboard Lamont's ships, and she cannot board them herself: U.S. Navy regulations at the time forbid women from taking part in research cruises.

## A Notch That Keeps Turning Up

Tharp works with Bruce Heezen, who collects the data at sea while she turns it, onshore, into topographic cross sections and then maps. By superimposing dozens of east-west profiles, she notices a detail that repeats: at the top of the mountain range running down the middle of the Atlantic, a narrow notch turns up on almost every cross section. It is not a measurement artifact. It is a continuous valley, sunk into the very center of the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.

## “Girl Talk”

When Tharp shows her map to Heezen and suggests he see in it a rift valley, a continuous tear along the ridge, consistent with the idea that the continents are moving apart, he refuses to believe it. He would himself recount, years later, that he took it for “girl talk,” and changed his mind only a year later, when an independent map of the Atlantic's seismic epicenters was laid over the notch Tharp had spotted and matched it exactly: the earthquakes followed precisely the same line.

## A Missing Piece of the Theory

The discovery lands at the right place and the right time. The theory of continental drift, proposed by Alfred Wegener forty years earlier, still lacked a convincing mechanism. An active rift valley, running the full length of a worldwide undersea mountain chain, offers exactly what was missing: proof of a place where oceanic crust is really spreading apart. Heezen presents the discovery with Maurice Ewing to the American Geophysical Union, in Toronto, in 1956, without Tharp's name on it; the complete physiographic map of the world ocean, drawn by hand by Tharp with the illustrator Heinrich Berann, would not appear until 1977.

## What the Anecdote Shifts

The phrase “girl talk” is not a legend embellished after the fact. It is an admission Heezen made himself, reported in a book about Lamont published in 1974. It says something fairly plain about how data can be dismissed because of who shows it rather than what it shows, before being recognized, a year later, for what it had been showing all along. Tharp would not board a research ship until 1968, sixteen years after drawing the line that would help tip an entire theory.

citation.texte: In three of the transatlantic profiles she noticed an unmistakable notch in the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, and she decided they were a continuous rift valley and told me. I discounted it as girl talk and didn't believe it for a year.

carte.punch: She had seen the rift; he took it for “girl talk.”
carte.idee: In 1952, Marie Tharp spots a rift valley in the middle of the Atlantic. Bruce Heezen, who gathers the data at sea, refuses to believe it for a year. He would admit himself that he took it for “girl talk.” The proof would come from seismic epicenters, lined up along the same line.

quiz.question: How did Bruce Heezen finally come to accept the existence of the rift valley Marie Tharp had spotted?
choix: By going to sea himself to check the relief of the seafloor
By recalculating the bathymetric profiles with a more precise method
By finding that an independent map of seismic epicenters followed exactly the same line
By consulting Alfred Wegener's published work on continental drift
quiz.explication: What swayed Heezen was not a new measurement of the relief. It was a completely independent map: that of the epicenters of Atlantic earthquakes, which followed precisely the same line as the valley Tharp had spotted. The coincidence between two independent sets of data made the rift valley impossible to dismiss.
